utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to turn into closed session or private session. Is there anyone in the public gallery? Can't see, no. Then the effect is still the same.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, may I first ask you to give your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Subotic, you were born when exactly and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th of April, 1941, in Turjak, municipality of Gradiska, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Subotic. Have you received a copy of the statement that was compiled by the legal officer of the Chamber and was translated into Serbo-Croatian and sent to your home on the 8th of June of this year? Did you receive that copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any corrections would you like to make to the statement as it has been put on paper by a legal officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is just a typo. I didn't have the opportunity of getting in touch with Mr. Zahar. Not everything was recorded in the sequence of our actual conversation. The beginning and the end of our conversation are not recorded in this report and they are very important for me. Further on, if this statement of mine is accessible to you and to the Defence and to the Prosecution, I don't see how they will know what kind of questions were put to me. In view of the practice I had earlier on, with the investigations Chamber of The Hague Tribunal, things were done quite differently. I would like to ask you something, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may first give you some information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This statement has been written down mainly for the purpose of having the most important information you gave during the interview on paper. The parties have also available the full transcript of the interview, so therefore this is mainly made for evidentiary purposes. And the parties have everything available to them. So therefore I would agree with you that not everything you said is reflected here, but everything you said is available to both the Prosecution and the Defence and the Chamber has read it as well. Therefore, I come back before I give you an opportunity to put a question to me, apart from typos, as you said, is there anything in this statement, apart from that it does not completely reflect the whole of the interview, is there anything you'd like to correct, which is wrong in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in conversation with Mr. Zahar, I did not have access to my statements made in 1997 and 1998. I didn't actually have them before me. Practically all questions pertained to those statements of mine. So I do not guarantee that I had the opportunity of repeating verbatim the statements I made and said in 1997 and 1998. That is why I ask you kindly, and I suggest to you, that at the hearing today, and during the following days, that when questions are put that are identical to the ones from my interview with Zahar, that previously I hear the answers I gave in 1997 and 1998. Could the transcript please be read out to me in my own language? As for that interview, or, rather, the statements I gave then, this was contemporaneous information. The events had happened only recently just before that. They were well supported and documented and there are several hundred of these documents that were handed over to this Tribunal in The Hague. I personally took part in this at the time, so I cannot guarantee that in this conversation with Zahar, I repeated verbatim what I said then, and I absolutely and fully stand by the statements I made then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Subotic, when the comparison of the earlier statements with the statement you gave just a couple of weeks ago raises some questions, at least as far as the Chamber is concerned, we'll put to you what your earlier statement said and what you said in your new statement, and of course the Chamber is aware of the lapse of time between the first statement you gave and the statement you gave in May 2006. So that's well understood. I come back -- I didn't hear you say that you'd like to make any specific corrections to the statement as put on paper. And my next question would be whether you'd like to add anything which you consider important before formally adopting this statement as your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to ask for a correction to be made or rather there are two mistakes on page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's page 5 in your language, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slowly tell us what is wrong in your language so that the interpreters can tell us what -- what it is and that we can check whether it's a mistake in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I presume that Mr. Subotic's copy is also identified with paragraph numbers. Perhaps he could identify in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Page 5. What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Line 3 in paragraph 17. It says here that I was deputy president of the municipality in Banja Luka as a Lieutenant. Not as a Lieutenant, but as a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in English, Mr. Subotic, it reads, "as a Colonel." So then it needs correction only in the version in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. And the other correction you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the last sentence in the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It reads as follows, "In the former Yugoslavia, I was elected as JNA representative from Banja Luka. I was elected as a member of the municipal government." Not as a member of the municipal government but as a councilman in the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean municipal assembly or -- I don't know what -- we always heard that an assembly is called a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can look at it that way. I was just a councilman. That is to say I was an elected official. It's not much of a post. It's not much of an office. It's just a temporary office in the political establishment. I was a member of the military. That was my profession. Whereas this word "member" in my language means that one belongs only to a particular sphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll correct that then as well. Any other correction needed, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, page 7, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the last sentence, it says - this has to do with Mr. Krajisnik - "If he had any private connections, I don't know of that. But he had no powers to issue any orders to anybody." And it is supposed to say if he had any private connections, I don't know about that, but he had no powers to issue any orders to anyone. No one was obliged to act upon his orders. There is a difference between decision and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The word "order" is used in English so it seems that for our understanding of your testimony, there is no need for correction, but we'll need to have a look, in view of your comments to the original, to the B/C/S translation, because the -- this statement was drafted in English first and then translated into B/C/S. I suggest to the parties that we'll invite Mr. Subotic to, once he has -- I come to that at a later stage. Mr. Subotic, you said these were the corrections you'd like to make. We'll take care of that. Is there anything you would like to add which you say this is very important? Of course, you couldn't add the whole history of what happened at the time but if you say, "I should add this because otherwise it gives a wrong impression of what I stated," then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, right now I do not have the opportunity to think of anything like that, but please, through your questions, if you feel that it is necessary to add something or to further clarify or explain something, please go ahead. I make myself available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that. I suggest to the parties the following, that we invite Mr. Subotic to sign the statement and ask a number to be -- exhibit number to be assigned to it, but to do that only once the corrections have been made, especially in the B/C/S, because there seems not to be a major problem as far as English is concerned. And therefore to proceed on the basis of the confirmation Mr. Subotic has now orally given. Is that an agreeable way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, the small corrections will be made and then the document will be given to you to be signed and will then become part of the evidence. I'll not proceed because we are not going to ask you to repeat everything you said. It's on paper. It will be in evidence. We have additional questions but I'll first read for the public a summary of your statement, which does not cover everything but which gives at least to the public a fair impression of what is approximately the content of your statement. But before doing so, Mr. Registrar, could you please assign an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be C3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: C3 will be the number. Then a copy of the document, have you received already a copy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's -- I don't know whether you insist on having -- well, once it has become an exhibit, then of course you'll get another copy, the new one, with mainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour mean the summary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Oh, we -- no, we've got that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've got that. No, you haven't got any of the summary. The summary has been prepared. I'll read out the summary and as always, the summary is not the evidence but is mainly to inform the public. And the statement will then be admitted under Rule 89(F) once signed. I nevertheless proceed already with the summary of the witness statement given the answers and the small corrections only the witness insisted upon. The summary of your statement, Mr. Subotic, before we put any further questions to you is as follows. In 1992, you were a deputy commander of the military school of tank units in Banja Luka. Professor Koljevic came to Banja Luka to ask you to serve as Minister of Defence. You went to Pale on the 8th of April 1992 to establish the Ministry of Defence. You remained the Minister of Defence for about a year. The first step you took as Minister of Defence was to draft the law on Defence and the army. The role of the Minister of Defence was mainly political. His duties were strictly limited. The Ministry of Defence was not in the chain of command of the military so the Minister of Defence did not make any decisions relating to command in the army. You did not receive any combat reports. The army was not obliged to provide any such reports to you. You stated that in the period, the 8th of April 1992 to the 12th of May 1992, the Bosnian Serb armed forces were not properly organised. There was no Supreme Command. The units were self-organised. In the following period, namely from the 12th of May 1992 to the end of 1992, you reported only to the government and to the Supreme Commander, that is the president of the republic. You stated that the Bosnian Serbs had no plan prior to the conflict to seize territories. You said that there was a lot of justified fear in the Bosnian Serb population and that the efforts of the Serbs were directed at preserving Yugoslavia. You had a good relationship with Mr. Krajisnik. You stated that there was no crossover of your powers and that Mr. Krajisnik's duties were strictly defined. He appeared at various meetings in his capacity as president of the assembly. Mr. Krajisnik had no powers to issue any orders whatsoever. He simply chaired the meetings of the assembly and he signed the enactments it passed. As Minister of Defence, you disagreed with the way General Mladic conducted military affairs, which led you to offer your resignation to the Bosnian Serb Assembly in August 1992. The problem with Mladic, according to you, was that he acted as commander of the Main Staff. You warned the assembly you could not work under two commanders at the same time, namely Mladic and Dr. Karadzic. You describe Mladic as pig-headed, stubborn, obsessed with himself, and not caring much about other people's opinions. Intellectually you felt closest to Prime Minister Djeric, Foreign Affairs Minister Buha, and President Karadzic. On the proliferation of arms you stated that about one-third of the material at the Banja Luka school, of which you had been the commander, ended up in the hands of the ARK administration in Banja Luka and was used locally by the Serbs in Banja Luka. You stated that the power to issue decisions rested with the Supreme Commander, which was the president of the republic, but he made decisions after consultation with members of the Supreme Command. Mr. Krajisnik was involved in military strategy only in his capacity as member of the Supreme Command. As for strategic operations, they were prepared by the Main Staff. Mladic was in charge of them. He submitted them to the Supreme Command for information. You also stated that the regions which formed in Republika Srpska had no military powers as of the 12th of May 1992. As for the month before that, they relied on Territorial Defence units, but during that period there were no major military operations. You stated that Vojin Vuckovic, leader of the Yellow Wasps, paramilitary group, visited you in Pale in the second half of July 1992. You had by that point drafted a presidential order to the effect that as of the 12th of May, all armed units were to be placed under the command of the army of Republika Srpska. You explained to Vuckovic that paramilitary units would not be allowed to exist. In your statement, you deny having direct knowledge of any illegal camps in Republika Srpska. You had heard from the media about Manjaca and Omarska camps but you also believed that some of that information was fabricated. The President of Republika Srpska issued an order to have the claims about these camps checked. You stated that you were not aware of any attack by Bosnian Serb forces on the village of Glogova on the 9th of May 1992, nor did you know of the alleged indiscriminate shelling of Sarajevo between the 15th and the 20th of June 1992. If Radovan Karadzic had issued an order to shell Sarajevo, you would have known about it, you stated. You also had not heard about the Japra Valley operations in late May 1992, during which about 4.000 persons from Muslim settlements were allegedly relocated to the village of Blagaj Japra by Serb forces. If there was such an operation, you stated, there could have been absolutely no connection between it and the civilian authorities in Pale. One incident you had heard about involved the mass killing of Muslim detainees at Koricanske Stijene. You stated that Dr. Karadzic received a report on this incident from the Banja Luka MUP. He convened an ad hoc session of the Presidency. You were ordered to go to Banja Luka to make inquiries and report back, which you did. This, Mr. Subotic, concludes my summary of your statement. The Judges have a few supplementary questions for you. So therefore I'd like to put those questions to you. I'd first like to direct you to paragraph 24 of your statement. Have you got the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You talk in paragraph 24 of your statement about the Bosnian Serb Assembly session of the 12th of August 1992. For the parties this is P583, tab 87. The transcript will be handed to you by Madam Usher, and I'd like you to read -- I'd like to read to you a passage from that transcript and ask you to comment. I start reading at the bottom of page 57 in English. And that would be in B/C/S, Mr. Subotic, part of the speech you delivered, which starts on page 54 in the B/C/S and then it's approximately one page further down. I'll read a portion of you speaking. You said, "Firstly, let me tell you this. Nobody informs me about anything relating to things that are going on in the army." Mr. Subotic, have you found the portion I'm reading at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Secondly," and I continue quoting you, "Secondly, I do not take part in any decision-making regarding the use of the army of the Serbian Republic. I cannot issue any orders to the SR army. I'm not in a position to fulfil my basic duties towards the government, which requests that I provide information daily as well as suggestions and so forth. As Defence Minister, I've not been involved in any negotiations on behalf of the Serbian Republic government regarding either military or any other issues. I've never been consulted regarding that. All my appearances before the public as Defence Minister were based on my personal feelings and on what I had found out personally. I had no official support in that." And then in the next paragraph, I continue quoting you, "With the army Main Staff, I had little or no contact at all. As Defence Minister, I've never spoken to the commander of the Main Staff. Very rarely did I have contact with other members of the command, and only when it was necessary from their side. It was not even possible for me to get in touch with them until a month ago." A bit further down in this speech you delivered, you say that you replied to General MacKenzie that you were in the field most of time and then you say and I quote you again, "Let me tell you that I toured all the front lines of the Serbian Republic on my own initiative, unannounced, without escort, without reception." My first question to you is the following, Mr. Subotic. Could you tell us how many staff were employed at the Ministry of Defence in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it was a relatively small number, around 30, I believe. At the ministry itself. At the offices of the ministry, because there were local organisation military departments, military districts, scattered all over the republic as branches of the ministry, in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us was it divided in sections these approximately 30 people? And could you tell us what sections there were in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a deputy. I had a section for logistics or, as we call it, rear support. I had a section for finance, a legal section, a section for mobilisation, and personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they staffed equally or were there great differences? Section on logistics, do you remember approximately how many people were employed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For finance? Similar or different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Finance, three or four people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Legal section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another three or four people, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That section had a little more staff, around ten, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to five people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your speech, which I quoted from before, you said that you obtained your information personally, without official support. What type of information are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information related to the army and the leading of certain operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you go about to obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was obtained mainly from reports received by the Supreme Commander, that is the president of the republic, and parts of those reports and requirements expressed in them were forwarded to the ministry in the form of requests to deal with certain issues, or if the army was making certain requirements of the government concerning supply, to meet the needs of the war, then the Prime Minister would give me that for my review, or I would get information from parties, individuals, who would address me individually in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This sounds a bit different from the beginning of your statement, where you said, "Let me tell you this. Nobody informs me about anything relating to things that are going on in the army." Whereas from your answer, I now hear that you obtained your knowledge, you obtained your information, mainly from reports received by the Supreme Commander, the president of the republic, and that parts of those reports were forwarded to the ministry. Could you explain where you said that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That relates only to the statements that had to do with the Ministry of Defence, logistics, mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do then understand that you say the information you gathered yourself was information not about logistics but about operational issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For instance, when I had occasion to make some tours to see how people lived, what kind of food is available, but without the commander of the Main Staff, I did not even have permission to tour certain positions where units, combat units, were positioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier, when I asked you about what kind of information you were referring to, you said information related to the army and the leading of certain operations, which I understood to be at least information about operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in terms of supply and in terms of logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you didn't even have permission to tour certain positions where units were positioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your speech at the assembly meeting, you said you had never spoken to the commander of the Main Staff and that you very rarely had contact with other members of the command, but also that you toured all the front lines of the Serbian Republic. I'm trying to -- I'm seeking clarification on the issue of you touring the front lines where you said you were not even allowed to go some places and needing permission of military commanders who you hardly had any contact with. Could you clarify on this point your answers, both as we find it in the statement and -- in your -- in the speech, observations you made there, and the answers you just gave to my questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, Your Honour, I was a general, and Minister of Defence. Often times, I wore a uniform and I put on my uniform only when I appeared in the vicinity of military units or when I toured. It was only natural for me to make appearances because I was their Minister of Defence at various ceremonies, taking of oath. It was ex officio, under the legislation, my duty to appear there. So I would go occasionally to make such an appearance. It was my moral duty to go there to see how people -- how personnel is supplied, how well they are supplied, whether our shipments are reaching them. But I did not have occasion, and I did not have the right, to visit the units that were involved in skirmishes and battles. The rule is that nobody can visit the front lines where battles go on without special permission, special escort, et cetera. So I went to visit only certain defence lines where personnel was positioned for a long time, in bunkers, et cetera. Those were the tours I made, and perhaps I also visited commands of certain units that were not directly in combat positions, but somewhere in reserve so I was never anywhere close to the range of fire, so to say. It's not necessarily what I would have preferred, but that's the way it was, and one of the reasons why I eventually resigned was this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us one or two examples of a place where you went and where you at such occasions went to the troops, although not that close that you went to combat positions? Could you give us one or two examples, without giving a full description of the whole tour, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll try. I have a very vivid memory of my tour of the units in Majevica, on the Gradacac line, going to some other places, Gradacac, Pelagicevo for instance, that's Mount Majevica. The units positioned there were not involved in combat at the time I visited. They were in a state of anticipation, expectation. I found them in trenches. I saw what kind of supplies they had, how they were dressed, how they were fed. I talked to soldiers and I remember I was surprised, it was a typical case, I was surprised to see a significant number of Muslim soldiers in the Serb army in those trenches and I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you went there and in what municipality could I locate Mount Majevica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Bijeljina. And when approximately did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August, approximately. It was a summer month, but I am not sure. It could even have been the beginning of September, but it was warm, relatively warm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your speech, you also said that -- the speech I quoted from -- that it was only in July 1992 that you were able to have contact with members of the army command. What made such contact possible suddenly in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was probably the result of my complaint submitted to the Prime Minister, because I have already mentioned that the Prime Minister wanted me to make certain proposals and it was probably the case that at one of the preliminary sessions I was forced to answer I cannot say anything because I am not familiar with the situation and I suppose that after that he talked to somebody in the Main Staff. At any rate, he told me, "Go there, evaluate the situation." So there were no obstacles and no delays then. I toured one unit on the bank of the Sava River between Brod and Svilaj because those units were holding positions on that side of the river, the Serb side. That's the right bank of the Sava River. And I toured a rather large area in that region, where two brigades were positioned, holding that line on the right bank of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more precise? What region that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely speaking between Orasje, up to Brod, approximately. It's a line perhaps 30 kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found that in the northwestern part, near to the Croatian border. Is that approximately the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Sava River was our border with Croatia, so on this side, the Bosnian side, units of the Banja Luka Corps were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, while we are talking about this subject, and to follow the same line of questioning asked of you by the Presiding Judge, you said, "[In English] I did not have permission to tour certain combat units where units were positioned." [Interpretation] And you've also added, "[In English] I had no right to visit the units that were involved." [Interpretation] Isn't that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first question is as follows, therefore: Where was it written that you did not have the right to go and visit the units that were involved in the combat? Was there a provision, a formal provision, which prohibited you from going there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no formal regulation but if I appeared at the boundary of that region, such a region, I would be stopped by a military police unit or some other unit and cautioned me that according to the orders of the Main Staff, all entry into that region, into that zone, was prohibited to everyone, and if I said that I was Minister of Defence and that I should be able to visit, they would reply that they had explicit orders and they cannot let me in. So I gave up at that point because I did not want to put that soldier in a position where he would have to answer for disobeying orders, and I would then accordingly report to the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in some cases you went to areas where there was combat and you were refused entry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did try. I did try. But I was not able to pass. And in those areas where there was no combat, where units were only deployed, there was no such prohibition. So I managed, in several locations, to tour such units because nobody stopped me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how many times did you try? How many times did it happen? How many times were you there and you got -- you were stopped and not allowed to enter a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure any more I can give you the exact number but I believe I was stopped and not allowed entry at least ten times, and I regularly reported that to the Prime Minister, who then reported to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did it ever happen that you asked authorisation from the commander or from the -- from the Main Staff, to allow you to go where the combat areas were situated? You had the legitimate right as Minister of a war to go and see what was going on. You could have asked for an authorisation, couldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sense of honour did not allow me to submit to such humiliation. As a Minister of Defence I was not supposed to ask the commander of the Main Staff for anything. I had contacts with the Prime Minister and the president of the republic, and I could not allow that man to manipulate me as he pleases. Whenever I presented that issue, whenever I raised that issue at sessions, however, one of such sessions was attended by General Mladic, he told me, "You, Minister, take care of ammunition, blankets, and food. Don't concern yourself with operations. That's not your business." And that's when I decided to resign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you -- when you were touring, how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled with a jeep, with this one man in the jeep, a driver. I had no escorts, no security men, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you use a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was not made available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, it's time for a break. I'll move to another subject after the break. We'll have a break of approximately 25 minutes, and it may be that during the break already the new version of your statement with the small corrections is ready for signature. We'll see that after the break. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, the corrected statement has been prepared. I'd like to invite you not necessarily to do this right away but to sign the cover page in B/C/S and to initial all the following pages at the bottom and then give it back to us, perhaps after the next break. I take it doesn't make that much sense to ask Mr. Subotic to sign or to initial the English version because I take it that he would not be able to read it, at least it's not the statement as he -- he didn't give the statement in that language. Then we will ask the interpreter and Mr. Zahar, the assistant to Mr. Zahar, to sign the English versions and then it's in evidence as C3. Mr. Subotic, I'd like to continue with the questions. Let me find it. Yes. The speaker that came after you, Mr. Subotic, on this 12th of August assembly session was Dr. Karadzic, and then after Dr. Karadzic, it was a certain Mr. Bijelic that spoke. You'll find that on page 61 of the English. First of all, could you tell us who was or is Mr. Bijelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, right now I cannot say for sure. I can't remember. As far as I can remember, it was an MP. But I don't remember his name. I know his face, not a very tall man. Believe me, I don't know. I don't know what municipality he was from, from which municipality he came as a deputy, and was it from Krajina itself, Dubica, something like that, but believe me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll read to you part of the speech Mr. Bijelic gave. He said, "Many things are not good in the army. This was my experience. I was hoping that we would be talking about this issue today and I thought this was a result of that. Many armies are going across our battlefields and our Serbian Republic, and I don't know whom they belong to. They are fighting their private wars and we don't know whom they are doing it for. I thought Mr. Subotic would say something about this. This could be very important reasons, in my opinion, about which we need to talk today. I know how the army was created. However, at this moment, when we have the army, when we have the War Presidency, my question is, who needs paramilitaries? Whose are those paramilitaries? Whose war are they fighting and who for? I want to hear more about this and I would ask Mr. Subotic to say something about this." Now, Mr. Subotic, as it happened, you did not get a chance to give an answer to Mr. Bijelic because the discussion in the assembly moved on to other matters. But those questions put by Mr. Bijelic, how would you have answered them if you have had a chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more or less along these lines: We established the army on the 12th of May. Actually, the decision was passed on that day, but the army itself was established formally only around the 20th, or to be quite frank, only towards the end of 1992, because we were not in a position to bring all of this in order within a week or a month. You know already from my statements that the legal regulations governing the army were all written very precisely and on time. They were all actually ready on that day when the army was supposed to be established. I can claim with full responsibility that these regulations reached all units, all military formations, that is. I can say that with certainty because that was verified through a certain administrative system, through command and so on. However, I cannot guarantee that all of that was carried through on time. You see, Mr. Bijelic was actually right in saying what he said at that point in time, when this assembly was held. That was right after the establishment of the army so the period of time involved was very short. Not all units had been placed under the control of the JNA. Oh, I beg your pardon, not the JNA but the army of Republika Srpska. However, with a certain degree of certainty, I can claim that by the end of 1992, the system was established, say, up to a degree of 90 per cent, as far as subordination is concerned and so on. There were perhaps some exceptions, but generally speaking, in a war situation, exceptions are not rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are talking about units. You said not all units had been placed under the control of -- and then you corrected, the army of Republika Srpska. What kind of units do you have in mind, if you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I explained it in my statement. If you read my statement, and I suppose you did, that before the official establishment of the army, these were groups or let's call them units, platoons, small units, of the Territorial Defence in various towns, municipalities, local communities. Throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only in Republika Srpska. You know that the Territorial Defence existed in Yugoslavia as a system. There was a law on Territorial Defence or, rather, on All People's Defence and Territorial Defence and civil defence or rather social self-protection, I beg your pardon. All of that was regulated by law. So these were practically formations of the republics and the municipalities but they were not subordinated to the Yugoslav People's Army. That is to say that in this kind of organisation, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke out. Of course, the Muslim units were established in their own areas, their own groups were established there, and the Serb units in their territories and so on. When I said units I was referring actually to these groups that had been established outside the system of the army. That is to say before the army had been already -- had been officially established. That is what was meant, not brigades, battalions or any such thing. Quite simply, formations in towns that were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You specifically mentioned Territorial Defence units. Would you include police units as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would include police units, because police units were local units, too. And they were local in the political communities, that is to say in the municipalities and the republics and so on. In the law on all National Defence, it was stated that in a case of war, all armed groups should be involved in a formation, that is to say that they should be placed under the command of the army. Up until then they tried to make do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you said that these units had not yet been subordinated, would you also include paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where Mr. Bijelic was talking about the existence of multiple, roaming armies fighting private wars, you said he basically was right, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was basically right. Perhaps not in each and every detail. You see, that is the way he felt. That is the way he experienced things. For instance we have those yellow wasps there and whatever else. They cannot be considered units. These were groups consisting of five to ten men that did something on the basis of, well, I've already spoken about that and when this person came to see me -- well, any way, this is what Mr. Bijelic thought. One cannot say that this was a mass phenomenon. Perhaps, as he travelled through the republic he came across these small groups which were perhaps not even fully in uniform, and then perhaps he saw something in their conduct and so on, but all orders had been issued, everything had been regulated very precisely. No doubt about that. I know about that because I personally worked on this. There was control, but, gentlemen, this was a very short period of time. I don't want to shift the blame to anyone else now, but all of us who were in charge were responsible for this. But it was a war. I hope that you know a lot about this war and all wars. Even today the most powerful world organisations and the greatest powers of the world are not in a position to control certain organisations. So we didn't manage to do that either over a short span of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you said, "all of us who were in charge were responsible for this," what did you exactly mean with "this"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that period of time, during which these groups had to be squeezed in, in order to be under the command of the army. That's what I meant. Because you know, for example, in those days, there were even certain arrests of some of these groups, say those yellow wasps and they had some other kind of names that they gave themselves, so the president of the state, the Commander-in-Chief, issued an order, I know that you have that, I personally took part in the handing over of this documentation, and in this order the MUP, the Serb MUP, was ordered to arrest all armed persons who did not have military documents, to disarm them, arrest them, and for them to be treated accordingly, to be placed under the jurisdiction of the military and so on. I cannot guarantee that this was done precisely, expeditiously. I think that this is what Mr. Bijelic was alluding to when he took part in the discussion. That's why I'm saying that he's right; if he saw that, then it was correct. I am not doubting what he said in any way. I have no doubts. Perhaps he did indeed see a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "By the end of 1992, we achieved approximately 90 per cent of that goal to have all units subordinated." Could you tell us by August, at the time of this assembly session, how far had you -- what progress was made? Could you give us a percentage, approximately of we then did 50 or 70 or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think objectively speaking, that it should be about 70 per cent. I can tell you one thing, that after this assembly, it was taken a lot more seriously, because this was, well, a slap in the face, if I can put it that way. My resignation and everything else. And this affected the situation and improvements were made a lot faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you were touring, did you observe it with your own eyes as well, what Mr. Bijelic describes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To tell you the truth, in three or four cases, I had occasion to familiarise myself with the existence of three or four groups, like for example the white wasps and also in Sarajevo there was this other group. I don't know what its name was. About ten or so men. I was personally tasked with this, to go there and to get things in order and indeed I went there, talked to them, and this was all regulated within a single day. As for the Sava and other areas that I toured, I did not come across any such cases. In Bijeljina, there weren't any either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 24 of your statement, you say, and I quote, "I disagreed with the way General Mladic conducted the affairs and commanded over the army. So as a professional I did not want to carry on that way and I submitted my resignation." Could you give us some more detail about your disagreement with General Mladic's conduct of military affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I presented some characteristics of General Mladic here. For example, I'll give you this one particular example, it so happened that it happened on this very day, Vidovdan, Saint Vitus Day. That is the patron saint's day of the army of Republika Srpska. I hope that you're aware of its historical significance. That's when the battle of Kosovo started. When the first Saint Vitus Day of Republika Srpska was commemorated, it's a patron saint's day. Well, it wasn't that there was a large scale war going on yet at that time, so we had this celebration at Sokolac, military celebration, an official state organisation. General Mladic reviewed the troops, as he commanded the army, and I was also asked to review the troops together with him but I was not invited to stand on the stage with him. Look, I am not a person who enjoys this kind of glory. I would never want to be a commander of an army because in my heart of hearts I'm an anti-militarist person although I was a military man all my life. He did not offend me in this way but he offended the army and all of those present because I know who General Mladic is. He's a robust personality. He's a man who thinks that he's the only one who is smart, that he's the only one who knows things and that the rest of us are just riff-raff. That's the way he behaved. I knew that he and I were not on the same line. He was afraid of me because I looked at the truth and I indicated to the state leadership what his wrong conclusions were, what his arrogance was like and so on and so forth. So there are other things as well. But believe me, I tried to evade a conflict. As you saw, at this assembly, I did not say anything bad about General Mladic. I said a few concrete facts, quite frankly, but I did not want to be the person that would lead to discord. Who am I to lead to discord within a nation? I believed in God and I still believe in God. I have a different view of the world. I have a different view of life than Mladic does. So we were ideological opponents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- you said, "He was afraid of me because I looked at the truth and I indicated to the state leadership what his wrong conclusions were." Let me first ask you, when you are referring to the state leadership, who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had in mind those who were in contact with me while I was minister in the government and later President Karadzic when I was his adviser. I've already said here in my statement - perhaps you noticed that? - the army of Republika Srpska had regulations that it could rely upon in conducting a war. It was the rule of regiment, brigade, division, which was the basis of the Yugoslav People's Army, and all of us officers were trained along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have a more precise answer. You said all those -- those who were in contact with me while I was a minister in the government. I would like to focus on that period of time. Who were in contact with you that you considered to be persons, and just mention them by name, or by category, that you thought belonged to the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as the army is concerned, and that specific question about my relationship with Mladic, well, specifically with regard to that particular question, I had the opportunity of having contacts with the Prime Minister of indicating certain things to him, certain disagreements, and the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic. I didn't go beyond that circle, as far as those questions were concerned. As regards other questions, logistics and so on, that did not have to do with command and control, I had contacts with other members of the government as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the wrong conclusions, what did you consider to be wrong conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what context? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said earlier that Mr. Mladic was afraid of you because you would indicate to the state leadership his wrong conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes, I understand. I understand. I forgot about that. Well, you know what, I mean, the state leadership, as far as I knew, the entire state leadership, tried, in every conceivable way, to reach a peace agreement, to have cooperation with UNPROFOR, with international representatives who were in Bosnia at that time and so on and so forth. The army always had a different attitude. In one statement, as far as I can remember, in 1992, you know, every soldier is taught that he should advantage wish his enemy in any school, in any country in the world that's the way things are so if a soldier views these things in an orthodox fashion it's the only thing he does. The army and General Mladic himself had views that were different from those of the president of the state, the government and so on. Even the deputies in the assembly. He wanted to accomplish his objective and his task. However, logically, the situation that we were in at that time could not allow that kind of thing to happen. And he always had this very Orthodox view of his objective, that he had to defeat his enemy, force him to capitulate and so on. Do you see what I'm saying? I viewed this as a political personage. I quite understand that there aren't any victors in any war. I always understood that. That is why -- well, that's what I meant when I said "his wrong conclusions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, you said Mr. Mladic was going for the military victory, whereas the state leadership wanted to achieve results through negotiations. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Absolutely. That's how I saw everything that was going on around me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you tell the state leadership that this was a wrong conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I did. Of course, I did. And they understood. For instance, President Koljevic was our contact person with the UNPROFOR because he had excellent English, and he was in charge of those contacts, and he was always the one who talked to those agencies and he always had to overcome certain resistance from the army, although I have to say that in certain situations, when international representatives were biased in favour of the other side, the army was sometimes right. General Mladic was sometimes right. Let's take, for example, the Mount Igman case. There is no dilemma in my mind about that. I'm telling you as a professional soldier, that operation was stopped only because Serbs had an advantage. Lord Owen did that and convinced the leadership, and Muslims wreaked havoc after that operation. They brought in the mujahedin and many other things, and that step led to many mistakes in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, if you know, who took that decision on Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which decision, to stop the operation led by Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who stopped the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karadzic made that decision. And that's when they quarrelled, Mladic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether Karadzic took that decision just on his own or whether he discussed the matter with others? Are you aware of the genesis of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. There was a session of the Supreme Command to discuss that issue because the decision was made very quickly, I think. He made that decision exclusively under the pressure of Lord Owen or maybe some false promises that the latter made. But I'm telling you as a soldier, that decision, and I stand by what I'm saying, if that decision had not been made, Serbs would have taken Sarajevo. The citizens of Sarajevo publicly demanded from Mladic to allow them to leave the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just mentioned the Supreme Command. I would like to draw your attention to the paragraph 30 and 31 of your statement because there, you mentioned Supreme Command which you say was an advisory body to the president of the republic. First of all, could you tell us when exactly the Supreme Command began to function? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just give me a second. I think I noted it down somewhere. I think it's somewhere in my first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If somebody could look through the statement, because I cannot read English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I'll read to you what is said there at a later moment. But my first question, since you mentioned that in your earlier statement, is when -- do you know when the Supreme Command began to function? I'll put to you later the details of the -- could you please first focus on my question? I'll take you to the relevant text, Mr. Subotic, later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember now how many months it took. I think it was towards the end of 2002. Sorry, 1992. I know it wasn't right after the army was established. It could have been even in early 1993. Several months later. It wasn't straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, as I said, I will take you to the relevant portion of your earlier statement. One second, please. Yes. I would like to take you first to your recent statement to paragraph 31. In paragraph 31 of your statement, you say that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in military strategy only in his capacity as member of the Supreme Command. But you also said that the Supreme Command seems not to have been established right after the formation of the army or at least about the establishment of the army, and this Chamber has received evidence that it was not established until the 30th of November 1992. Do you know whether Mr. Krajisnik had any involvement in military strategy prior to the date where the Supreme Command was established, so that is up to the end of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he was involved in anything like that, because quite frankly I wasn't involved myself. I became a member of the Supreme Command later, when Krajisnik was a member. I said approximately towards the end of the year, and you now confirmed it was indeed in November, and as far as I knew, it was simply not possible for him to be involved. Whether he had any talks with the president is something that I cannot say one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 32 of your statement, your recent statement, you again refer to the Supreme Command. Who did General Mladic report to about strategic operations, prior to the establishment of the Supreme Command, as far as you know? Because if that body was established only late November, to whom did he report prior to the establishment of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll be very frank, quite frank. I don't think he reported to anyone, and if he did report to anyone, it was only to President Karadzic. But this is my personal, intimate opinion. I don't think he reported even to him. It's my conviction. I don't have any evidence for it, but that's what I felt at the time, and I haven't changed, as far as that feeling is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your testimony would then be that he operated entirely on his own, without -- or is that a wrong understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that word "entirely on his own," I don't know how appropriate it is. But for the most part, in my personal opinion, he mainly operated on his own until the establishment of the Supreme Command. That is what I dare to assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would not reporting also include not receiving instructions, not receiving any orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. They consulted each other and agreed on certain things, as far as I know. For the most part I didn't take part in such consultations at the Main Staff. Primarily because nobody invited me, neither the commander nor Mladic but I know that they met, either at the president's office or at the supreme staff, and they discussed, in the beginning, pending the establishment of the Supreme Command, I don't know to what extent they managed to consult and agree and I don't know what they discussed, to be quite frank. However, once the Supreme Command was established I would be usually present and I was aware of what was being discussed and what kind of decisions and conclusions are made, so that I cannot tell you anything specific one way or another about the period prior to the establishment of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do understand from your answer that where you said that -- yes, "I don't think he reported to anyone and if he did report to anyone it was only to President Karadzic," and you now explained that they would consult and they would agree on matters, just the two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I think happened, until the Supreme Command was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to -- I'd like to refer to a paragraph from the statement and now I'm referring to your earlier statement, the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997. It is paragraph 30 of that statement, and I quote what you said there. You have it in English only but as I said before, I'll put to you, then, what was said so that you receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that going to get a number as a result, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment I'm just quoting from it. So whatever at this moment is -- but we can see whether it will be an exhibit, whether it will be in evidence, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I quote what you said then. "When the chief of the Main Staff submitted a proposal, the president, with his deputies, Koljevic and Plavsic, and the president of the assembly, and with either the Ministry of Defence or the Minister of the Interior or the body that controlled" and then there is a -- it's -- "would discuss the matter in a joint conference and then it would be adopted." And then you continue in paragraph 31, "This would happen with most military operations." And by contrast, in your statement you gave this year, in 2006, to the Chamber, at paragraph 31, so I'm now referring to your recent statement, you say that, and I quote again, "Mr. Krajisnik was involved in military strategy only in his capacity as a member of the Supreme Command which was an advisory body. So he could present his opinion, he was allowed to do it, but he had no powers to make these decisions." Could you please help me to understand, then, what role Mr. Krajisnik had? Was he a member of a group that approved proposals of the Main Staff or was he a member of a purely advisory body on military matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a transcript of my interview with the OTP of 1998, because in April 1998, in supplementary questioning they asked me that question, just as you put it now, and I will only repeat the answer I gave to them then, because I still stand behind it. It's from that statement of 1998. "The Supreme Command is an advisory body of the president of the republic, who is, pursuant to the constitution, the Supreme Commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 4, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, right. Oh, you have it? That's good. Shall I continue or will you read it for yourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can read it ourselves, but perhaps you give your answer. If you say it's the same answer we'll see whether it really is. So tell us, but it seems that you have read it. And let's also see whether it's exactly the same question that was put to you. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make this observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now it is going to matter whether these documents are going to be exhibited because either they need to be read into the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- or they need -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, just in that connection, I recall that the previous practice adopted to the best of my recollection, and that began during the course of the Prosecution case in chief, I think, was that the document would of course be given a number and then portions which were the subject of attention during the examination would become exhibited rather than the entirety of the document. If it's to be otherwise we should -- or if anyone is suggesting that another approach be adopted, we should all be aware of it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we had several discussions on whether to admit a document as a whole or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I wish to reserve the Defence position as to whether we want to cross-examine the whole of this -- these documents, and how practically to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No one -- if I may no one is suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that only at the very end of the testimony of the witness we would consider whether or not so the two -- not exclude any cross-examination on matters which are in this statement. Is that a correct understanding? Apart from other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, and keeping with the previous practice, I don't think there was any suggestion before and certainly not now that relevant aspects of any document would be excluded from use during cross-examination. The only issue is how much of the document was used during examination-in-chief or cross-examination and therefore what parts of the document would become exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I'll invite at least at this moment, Mr. Registrar, to assign an exhibit number to this interview which dates from the 4th of February 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be C4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the statement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the statement of course we could -- I mean, assigning a number at this moment of course is not a final decision on admission, admission as a whole or admission of portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would then, I take it, Mr. Registrar, be C5?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will would be the witness statement the 9th of December, the 11th of December and the 12th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing more to say at this stage. We put down a marker and clearly the matter will need to be resolved in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked during that -- you gave the answer I just stated during the interview in December 1997, and that is about the president with his deputies, Koljevic and Plavsic and the president of the assembly and with either the Ministry of the Defence or the Minister of the Interior would discuss the matter, the matter being a proposal submitted by the chief of the Main Staff in a joint conference and then it would be adopted. And then in the other -- the question I put to you is to clarify what you stated in paragraph 31 in your 2006 statement where you said that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in military strategy only in his capacity as member of the Supreme Command. If you refer to the answer you earlier gave, I would specifically draw your attention to the fact that in your 1997 statement you were referring to the president of the assembly, and you were referring to a joint conference with the president. Could you therefore tell us what now exactly the role was of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in this domain of military strategy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. President, just one remark, and I hope you will take it into account, in this paragraph 31 of my statement from May this year, when I was interviewed by Mr. Zahar, I absolutely give priority to my statements from 1997 and 1998 because in this statement I only answered some additional questions. I hope you will appreciate that because I do not change anything in my statements of 1997 and 1998, and I stand by every word, and, please, take into account that 11 years later, I could not remember everything precisely, whereas in the prior statements from 1997, 1998, I carefully revised every word and every page. You see that in the additional interview made by the OTP, they sought clarification of that statement which includes the paragraph 31 in English that you've read out to me. Three months or maybe four months after that, from April to December, I gave a clarification. That means that to the best of my knowledge, Krajisnik, as the president of the people's assembly, was involved in military strategy only when he became a member of the Supreme Command. I claim with full responsibility that I have no information and no knowledge about his possible involvement before he became a member of the Supreme Command. He may have attended an occasional meeting, just as I did, but I had no say, and no importance, as a visitor, whereas a member of the Supreme Command I was entitled to voice my opinion, to defend it and so on. I'm trying to explain here, to the investigator, that the Supreme Command was an advisory body of the president of the republic. After I ceased to be Minister of Defence, I became an advisor to the president of the republic. And forgive me in advance, Your Honour, for making this comparison, it is questionable whether you should listen to every piece of advice Mr. Zahar gives you because I had advisers as well but it was ultimately up to me to decide whether I was going to listen to them or not. I wanted to -- this to be perfectly clear. I have no information that, prior to the establishment of the Supreme Command, some other people were involved. Maybe they did but I have no knowledge about it and I cannot say one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us until when Mr. Koljevic was a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic was a member of the Presidency, I think until several months before his death, and -- to be honest, I cannot remember precisely. Until approximately the session that discussed the Vance-Owen plan, around that time. I cannot be more precise than that because Mr. Koljevic, as far as I know, because I attended that session of the assembly that attended the Vance-Owen plan attended by that Greek and all the other visitors and Milosevic too, Mr. Koljevic then differed from everybody else in the Serb leadership. He took a completely different line, and he was also ill at that time. I cannot give you a precise answer to that question but up until that time approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, in your statement of 1997, you said that the matter would be discussed in a joint conference. Who exactly were joined in that conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. What conference, what commission? Can you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read it to you. The statement reads, "When the chief of the Main Staff submitted a proposal, the president, with his deputies, Koljevic and Plavsic, and the president of the assembly, and with either the Ministry of Defence or the Minister of the Interior or the body that controlled would discuss the matter in a joint conference and then it would be adopted." So you're talking about a joint conference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I said so in my statement and I can confirm now as well, President Karadzic for the most part -- well, I'm talking about the period of time before the establishment of the Supreme Command, lest there be any misunderstanding. So in that period of time, since President Karadzic did not have this advisory body, the Supreme Command, it was his custom to consult someone, some of these people that I mentioned. I had no insight unless he invited me too. It was his custom to invite people over to consult with him. I know that he definitely consulted with the two, Koljevic and Plavsic, as members of the Presidency. That I know for sure. They were invariably there. As for the rest of us, including me, including Krajisnik, the Minister of Police, and so on, we were called in every now and then, depending on what he wanted, what he needed, well, I cannot make any assumptions now when it was that he invited us and when he did not invite us. It was his personal decision. As for that part which I explained then is what I tried to explain further to you now, if you've been able to follow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the portion I just read from your statement refers to the period in which the Supreme Command was not yet established. Judge Hanoteau was a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you know in what circumstances the Supreme Command was formed? Following what event, following which meeting, following what discussion was it created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you. You know what, after the Igman operation -- well, at that time we didn't have a Supreme Command. I dare say perhaps I'm not right but in my view so I'm restricting myself to myself only, there was a serious division between General Mladic and the Supreme Commander, a rift. I think that Karadzic then realised that quite simply, under such circumstances, he should not, or he did not have the right to, I don't know really how to put this, that he should not make this -- these decisions on his own with Mladic. He should engage more people. The more people, the more wisdom. So it's not only two people that can make decisions. I think that that is what compelled him, Karadzic, as the Supreme Commander, to establish the Supreme Command, because that is customary practice in armies in the territory of Yugoslavia, in the Balkans, absolutely, and in war situations, that exists in many other armies around the world, perhaps the names are different but the purpose is the same. I think that that was the reason, Your Honour, for him to come to this conclusion to establish the Supreme Command. Karadzic realised that he had made a mistake, that he actually did what Lord Owen was trying to talk him into and I'm telling you this quite frankly as a professional, as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could it have been originated from the fact that General Mladic had to report to no one? You said, "To be very honest, I do not believe that he had to report to anyone, and if he did, it would have been only to President Karadzic. That is my personal belief, and I believe that he was not reporting everything to him any way." So the fact that he acted in such an autonomous way, in such an isolated way, that -- does that -- is that the reason why the Supreme Command appeared all of a sudden or was created, was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my personal belief. I have no proof nobody gave me that kind of explanation, Karadzic or anyone else but I personally think that that could have been one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever hear at the time when General Mladic was not reporting, was not telling what was going on, did you ever hear, did you ever understand, that military actions had not really matched the expectations of political powers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite put it that way, so not fully, but as for the way in which this was done, well I have my suspicions. You know what, there is a problem which is more profound. With the permission of the president I would like to explain. You will understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please just answer my question to begin with. Did you ever hear, do you know, of anything which would have made you believe that the military action went far beyond the political authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, on the basis of my own personal thinking, as a general. Because I myself never would have done that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it that you had heard? Please elaborate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- well, you know what, for example, I know of a particular operation, if you allow me I will give this concrete case, this operation that took place in Zepa when there was fighting for a repeater, a TV repeater. Well, I don't know if it was also a repeater for the communications system too. But General Mladic sent his deputy, General Milovanovic into that action at his own initiative. Quite specifically, this military unit from Pale fell into a Muslim trap, an ambush of the Muslim army, and there was a massacre that took place, a lot of people were killed. And there was a state of emergency in Pale. As a matter of fact, the president established a state commission to investigate the matter. I was on the commission, as were other people, but there was nothing to investigate. It was an unheeded operation. It was an operation based on poor military judgement, preparation, operation and so on. But by your leave, it is very important for me to say the following to you. As regards this autonomy exercised by Mladic, a mistake was made there. I said so in my statement. Perhaps you didn't understand, but allow me to explain. When the Main Staff was established I encountered my first problem as Minister of Defence. General Mladic was smart. He imposed upon the leadership of Republika Srpska that this should be called the Main Staff. Up until then, never such thing had ever existed in any army in the world. So he imposed this, that he should be appointed commander of the Main Staff on the 12th of May. That did not exist anywhere else in the world. So he's the commander and Karadzic is the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've already explained, in your interview actually, and thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question in that respect. You gave an example of General Mladic going beyond what he was expected by the political leadership to do, and it had a bad result. You said it was bad; militarily it was not well done. Did it ever happen that General Mladic went beyond what the political leadership wanted him to do with positive results, that is military success?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any concrete data. I have some thinking of my own, but I cannot support it with concrete data, although in my heart of hearts, I think there were some situations where things happened the way you had just put it. For example, in a concrete case, I've already said that I think that General Mladic was right as far as the Igman operation was concerned. That is what I think as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there, I do understand, he followed the instructions of the political leadership. The question was, and again is, whether there were any examples known of General Mladic going beyond what he was expected to do by the political leadership, having military success in doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know what? Now, I don't know whether this is a military success or whether it's a catastrophe. Now, that is debatable.
