But Srebrenica is one such example, because the political leadership did not ask Mladic for Srebrenica to happen. I know with certainty that there was no such directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me take you back. I'd like to focus on 1992 rather than on anything that happened at a later stage. Do you have any such example in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean -- and I'm now putting it in another way -- that whatever military action or military operation took place under the command of General Mladic did not go beyond what the political leadership wanted him to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not recall. I simply cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I invited you to give examples where he went further than the political leadership would expect him to. You couldn't give any such examples and I'm now asking whether that is to be understood as that he stayed within what the political leadership wanted him to do when instructions or -- were given or when the political leadership was consulted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, in 1992, there weren't any serious military operations except for operation Igman. Later, there are some examples, later, in the second half of the war, there are some examples that I know of but I don't know of any examples up until the end of 1992 except for Zepa. There is nothing that I could really indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's continue. At the end of paragraph 45 of the statement you gave to the Trial Chamber, the written statement, you say, and I quote, "I state that Radovan Karadzic never issued an order to shell Sarajevo because, if there had been such an order, I would have known about it." How can you be sure that you would have known about such an order in June 1992, if it would have existed, since from what I understand, you were not in the chain of command and you were not yet the adviser to Dr. Karadzic at that time? So how could you be so sure that he never issued an order to shell Sarajevo? And I'm talking about June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can just refer to this particular case, when in 1997 and 1998 we were preparing the requested documentation for the investigations Chamber, we were doing this from the archives of the president of the republic. I was a member of that team and we never found any such order in the archives. I'm talking about orders in writing. As far as I know, especially later - especially later - and I assume that that's the way it was beforehand too, President Karadzic did not give oral military orders. I'm not aware of any such case. That is why I was so unequivocal, that I would have known about this order, although I was not in a position to say at that time. But we offered from the archives all the orders that were there. On the very spot we offered that to the investigations Chamber and no such order was found, as far as I can remember. I know, for instance, that this shelling -- well, I know a lot of cases, Mr. Krajisnik does too, when from Sarajevo, from Igman and Bijelasnica, they were firing shells at our building where the Presidency worked or rather the state organs in Pale, and then certain units would respond with individual shellings, well, these were individual shellings too let me be quite clear from the Muslim side and then this was returned. In military jargon, this is called exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said that President Karadzic would never give oral military orders. Earlier you explained to us that before the Supreme Command was established in late November 1992, that General Mladic would consult with Mr. Karadzic and that -- I should find your words exactly, that -- I think you said but please correct me if I'm wrong, that they would then agree on matters. Would that mean that to agree on matters is something different from giving an order? Could it be that, for example, they would have agreed on this matter where you later did not find any written order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the Supreme Commander -- well, this is what he was advised too. I mean I advised him to that effect, and I gave him some military rules for him to read. Before some operations that are of a stronger nature, if I can put it that way, strategically or operatively, to speak in military jargon, he sought their advice first but then he signed the orders that they would prepare for him. That's why I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you for a second? You're talking about what period of time exactly? I'd like you to focus on 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entire period, from the establishment of the army, from the establishment of the army and later on the Supreme Command too, because then there were discussions at the Supreme Command, at Supreme Command level, so there was a discussion, but what would invariably follow would be his order. In some smaller operations, say like this one in Zepa, I'm not sure that there was an order involved that was issued by the president. I'm not sure that Mladic informed him about it either but this was not an operation. One unit, say, at company level took part in this - you know, not the Supreme Commander - decides about the participation of individual companies. He would decide when several brigade-level units were to be involved or units at corps level, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me now try to see whether I well understood the situation that existed before the Supreme Command was established in 1992. I do understand, but please correct me when I'm wrong, is that General Mladic and Mr. Karadzic would discuss operations, at least if there were major operations, and that as you said in your 1997 statement, to which you added today that that described the situation before the Supreme Command was established, that others, you specifically mentioned in your statement Koljevic, Plavsic, president of the assembly, Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Defence, were consulted, not at every occasion but these were the persons you specifically mentioned that were consulted, that this would then lead to a common understanding or an agreement between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic, and that that would be the basis for orders and, as you said, you're not aware of any orders given unless they were written down. Is that a correct understanding of what approximately happened, well, let's say, in 1992, up until late November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. I think that you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Subotic, we'll have another break for 20 minutes. Could you please have a look at the corrected statements, initial every page and sign the cover page in B/C/S? We'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to deal with a few very practical matters. Next Friday, this Friday, we'll have a bit of an irregular day. That is we'll start in Courtroom III at 11.00 in the morning, not at 9.00. We'll continue until 2.00 in the afternoon and then after a break of one hour, we'll be in court from 3.00 p.m. up until 6.00 p.m. So that's a bit of an irregular schedule for that Friday only. Then I have another request. During the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik on the 15th of June, two times reference was made to a visit of journalists, I think accompanied by Mr. Ostojic to camps, and reference was then made to an interview and a -- and/or an article, it might be the same, in Kozarski Vjesnik and it was then repeatedly said that this was among the material that we had. It's in your material, it says, on transcript page 25828, which was the last reference. And we have some difficulties in locating that Kozarski Vjesnik article or interview. If the parties could assist the Chamber in locating it, then that would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on our side the Defence, I will certainly do what we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the OTP that goes without saying, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. No immediate answer but we will look at it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then now continue, Mr. Subotic. In paragraph 46 of your statement, that's the next paragraph to the one I referred to before the break, in reference to the alleged displacement of thousands of Muslims in the Japra Valley, you state, and I quote, "They," meaning the groups that carried out attacks, "had absolutely no connection with the civilian authorities in Pale because, as a member of the government, I would have known about this." At the same time, we see that you complained to the assembly that you were left in the dark about many matters. How can you be so sure that you would have known about incidents occurring in municipalities such as the one, the alleged incident I just mentioned in the Japra Valley? So how can you be so sure that you would have known about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since this was about Krajina that was partially involved in the conflict at the time, partially, the information coming from municipalities and deputies from municipalities would come to Pale, the government, and occasionally even the assembly. So on account of that, I assert that as a member of the government, I would have known about that case, had it been discussed by the government. I'm not sure whether it is defined which period in 1992 it was. I don't remember whether Mr. Zahar put it to me. Can we specify which period that relates to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about June, July, 1992, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. President, by that time telephone and other communications had already been established with Krajina, so I personally think that this would have been known to the government or the MUP, which is part of the government after all, and that's why I was so determined in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say that you personally think that this would have been known to the government, whereas in your statement you said there was no connection with the civilian authorities in Pale because, as a member of the government, I would have known about this. It's not entirely clear to me yet what position you now take.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, Mr. President, this involves a huge amount of people, 4.000 people. It's not a small group, it's neither four nor 40. I believe that there is no municipal authority or police force in that area that could have kept this from the government or Pale. Since that was never a subject of discussion, ever, I can simply not conceive that something like that could have happened without anybody having been informed, whereas the communication lines were working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it now -- is your testimony that it could not have happened because you didn't know about it and such a massive operation was inconceivable without being known even at a distance or do you say they must have known about it when it happened but for whatever reason you were not informed about it, if you were not informed about it? And that's what you seem to say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot fathom that an operation on that scale or let's say event, not an operation, that an event on that scale could have happened without the authorities in Pale being informed in some way, and I was part of those authorities in Pale. That's the only thing I am saying. I have no information. The first time I heard of it was from a question put to me by Mr. Zahar. Until then I had never heard anything about that event, that version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're inclined to believe that it did not take place because you and others would have known about it, and you were not aware of it? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right. I'm inclined to believe that on that scale, something like that would -- could not happen without it being known. But I have no evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber received evidence which suggests that such an event did take place, and that is not just stories but that includes documentary evidence, that includes some pictures. So, therefore, if you say, well, hardly could have taken place since we didn't know about such a massive event, I just inform you that of course there was no finding from the Chamber in that respect but there is quite a bit of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what you're saying, but I do have reason to doubt that anybody in Pale was informed. I can simply not fathom that somebody could have been informed at Pale without raising a campaign on that issue. That's the only thing I'm saying. I cannot claim whether it happened or not, and if it happened, if you have evidence that it did, then all I can say is that I have no information and I have no way of explaining why that was not communicated. I'm telling you the first time I heard about it was in the form of a question put to me by Mr. Zahar. I had never heard of it before. You have to believe me. Neither then nor later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should -- I might have not correctly linked what we see in paragraph 46, and I think I should tell this to the parties at this moment, because the statement of the witness was not about any knowledge of displacement of thousands of Muslims but was about the connection of groups that carry out attacks with the civilian authorities. I think I should have been more clear that these are two different issues and, in view of the answers, what I said about the evidence I should have been more clear about what -- on what issue this Chamber received evidence, including documentary evidence, and pictures. I'll move on to the next subject but not until after Judge Hanoteau has put question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, after the war ended, within the months and the years that went by, were you aware of the fact that some incidents that could be interpreted as war crimes could have been committed without you having been informed of them when they took place? Or in other words, in the following years after the end of the war, did you ever discover that some events took place of which you had no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard of such things, but I didn't discover any of them myself. I read in the press. I found out from some other sources. From reactions by international organisations and so on, of course I knew and I heard of some such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how can you explain that you could have missed something like that at the time when these events took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could I know, Your Honour? How could I know? I'm trying to tell you all the things that happened on the territory of the republic, that were notified in any way to the leadership at Pale, resulted in some sort of response, reaction. I don't know of a single situation when the government in Pale was informed and failed to react. I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but if I could seek a little clarification about the last point Your Honour made before yielding the floor to Judge Hanoteau about paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. About 46, I -- there are two issues, I think, in paragraph 46. One is -- let me just -- I think I started the question about how the witness could be so certain as to the fact whether there was absolutely no connection between the groups that carry out the attacks with the civilian authorities in Pale. That's such not a problem but when I later referred to evidence this Chamber received, I had in mind photographs of buses, I had in mind not specifically evidence on the link between Pale and the group that carried out attacks, but I had something different in my mind and I therefore was a bit concerned that I would have created confusion. This is not to say that there is no evidence or no evidence whatsoever on the other matters but that's what I had in mind and was a bit afraid that there would be confusion as to evidence on the displacement of Muslims on the one hand side and on the links between the civilian authorities in Pale and the groups that carried out the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's essentially what I understood the Court to be saying. I rose because, for what it's worth, and I don't want to start a debate about that, but I was hoping that we could clarify that. I understood the witness's response to be, to implicate at least in part the size of the displacement, the issue of displacement and I looked at the statement again and the transcript to see if that was part of it as well, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I understood as well but at the same time I quoted his words on the links between attacks and the civilian authorities in Pale, and that could have created confusion and, being aware of that, that doesn't mean what the witness said about to what extent big events must have been known in Pale is a different matter but I just noticed that I was switching from one subject to another and I just wanted to make clear that I had some concerns about creating confusion. I'll move on. Mr. Subotic, this was just a procedural matter which might not be of primary importance for you. In paragraph 26 of your statement, you say that intellectually you felt most close to or you felt most respect for Prime Minister Djeric, Foreign Affairs Minister Buha and Dr. Karadzic. Did you feel the same intellectual closeness and respect for Mr. Krajisnik or was that different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, I had very few points of contact with Mr. Krajisnik, because from my field of expertise, he was of no interest to me because he was not making decisions, he was not issuing orders. Of course, we would meet at assembly sessions when I would come. Whereas the Prime Minister was somebody I met every day, I had to discuss all problems with him, and also the foreign minister, Buha, was also a member of the cabinet. I saw him every day, and the President Karadzic, both as head of state and Supreme Commander, was somebody I saw every day. And that's why I said what I said. I didn't mean to say that our relations were bad or anything. It's -- except that we had nothing that would link us in everyday work. I had no problem with speaker Krajisnik. I simply had no need to see him or discuss with him because he had nothing to do with my area of work, and I gave the answer to the question put to me by Mr. Zahar spontaneously. We were close, the people I enumerated, but I don't mean to say that I didn't like Mr. Krajisnik. He was a charming man, very witty. His demeanour in conducting the sessions of the assembly was very -- very good, but he was like that with everybody, not with me in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question is about paragraph 29 of your statement. You're talking about material that was taken from the Banja Luka military school. I have some very short questions on that. Could you tell us, when were these weapons removed from the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the beginning of the war, in April 1992. You see, before that, I used to be the commander of that school, before I took the office of Defence Minister. That used to be the school of armoured units of the JNA, which means that all tank crews got schooled there. It had a lot of equipment and teaching aids, but the Yugoslav army which was no longer JNA at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not specifically interested in further details about the school. But these weapons, were they stolen from the school? Were they removed? Were they shared on the basis of any agreement? I mean, removed under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, by that time I was already at Pale, serving as Minister of Defence, but I was informed by the president of the municipality, now late Mr. Radic, it was simply a reaction of the people, of citizens. When the army came to withdraw its equipment from the school, the people of Banja Luka took to the streets and came to the representatives of the army of Yugoslavia and told them that, "You can take your teaching aids and your staff but we have no units here and we have to defend ourselves. The war has started." And although I have no precise knowledge, but I think that about one-third of the equipment stayed behind. A part of it was given to the police in Krajina. Mostly APCs and lighter equipment and a couple of tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, on my earlier question, you said these weapons were removed from the school in April. When you described the circumstances, I do understand your answer to be that this was what was left behind when the JNA moved out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That school withdrew in April. Well, of course, there were some units who withdrew later, in the Sarajevo region that I know of, and throughout the republic, but that particular school, I know for certain, withdrew in April. I don't know the exact date. Many people left, the teaching staff, the equipment, computers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier said that it surprised you that there were at a certain moment still Muslims in the army when you were touring the separation lines. Here you say it all -- at least you say it -- your answer was about -- about Serbs who did get these weapons. Therefore I asked whether there was any agreement. Are you aware of any of these weapons ending up in the hands of non-Serb units or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, not from the school. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know any further details about how this happened? You told us already that you heard from it from the late Mr. Radic. Are you aware of any further details on how this weaponry ended up in the hands of the, as you said in your statement, ARK administration of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they simply left behind part of the weaponry, and the territorial units in the region of Krajina took it over. Some were formed later, some were already formed at that time, because there were no armed conflicts in Banja Luka in 1992, I can say that a -- considerable parts of Muslims inhabitants of Banja Luka remained in the Territorial Defence units there. Some of them are receiving war disability pensions. They are veterans of the previous war. But Banja Luka was a rather exceptional case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to paragraph 47 of your statement. You make reference there to the Koricanske Stijene incident which Dr. Karadzic asked you to investigate, and you describe an ad hoc meeting. Do you know who initiated the ad hoc meeting of the Presidency at which the Koricanske Stijene incident was discussed? Do you know who initiated that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who initiated that but the president told us that he had received a telegram or a report from the Banja Luka MUP, and he also got a call from the International Red Cross or some other international organisation, but I think it was the ICRC, who had the same information, so he gathered us all pronto, he was very angry, and as I understood from his reaction, he suspected a military unit of being the culprit. That military unit, what was its name, right across from Koricanske Stijene? Can anybody help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot. You're the witness. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Let me try. It's on the road to Vlasic. Maybe Mr. Krajisnik can remember what it was called, this particular place. I simply cannot remember right now. My mind has simply stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it comes back into your mind, please tell us, and if not, we'll have to do without. So you said the ad hoc meeting -- the ad hoc meeting was convened very quickly, you said. Have you any recollection on such ad hoc meetings of the Presidency to discuss current issues, whether they were convened on other occasions as well in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, up to that time, no, I don't remember any such case. Believe me. I do not remember any such case in that period of time. Perhaps there were some cases later, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not specifically talking about this type of case, but any current issue which would cause the Presidency to be convened, such a meeting to be convened to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. For example, I remember this particular case in Zepa. I think that was before this, or somewhere around that time. I'm not sure of the date now. When this thing happened in Zepa, I told you about that, when those soldiers were killed, the soldiers led by General Milovanovic, so there was an evening session when people were trying to decide what should we do? People reacted and the international organisations became involved too. Mr. Akashi and whoever else. I think there were about 54 fatalities involved. Please don't take my word for the actual number. It was a very painful situation. And that's the way they reacted, at least up until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did that happen more often that on the basis of some urgency coming up that a Presidency meeting was convened on very short notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could not say more often. Well, it didn't really depend on anyone. It depended on what would actually happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this Chamber has seen minutes or at least documents about Presidency meetings which takes place now and then a bit irregular now and then, sometimes two days after another, sometimes more time in between. These -- the Presidency meeting, as far as you were aware of, would that be very frequent or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as necessary, in my opinion, as necessary. If the situation called for a meeting, then there weren't any special pre-set times and it was done in a formal way. It was done in an ad hoc manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us how often you approximately attended meetings where the -- at least all the members of the Presidency were present in a small setting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say now. I was present when I was invited. Of course, I was not even aware of many meetings, but their custom was -- oh, I beg your pardon. Their custom was to invite some people who were required in a particular situation, who were supposed to help them by way of providing information, taking measures and so on and so forth. We, the rest of us, who were not on the presidency, were not invited that often. Well, perhaps I dare say that -- well, it depended on the situation. But, say, two or three times a month, maybe, that might be an average. But it depended on the situation. It had to do with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it just occurred to me that there was an issue previously with respect to 92 versus past 92. I don't know if that was a distinction -- I don't know that it's become --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to ask. Now, focusing on 1992, Mr. Subotic, you said two or three times a month. Did you say that in this period of time, when you were Minister of Defence, that you would be invited two or three times a month to attend a meeting of this character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately that would be it. Not that that's when meetings were held. I don't know. I'm sure that they were held more often. But how can I know how often they were being held?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you were invited two or three times a month during that period of time when you were a Minister of Defence to attend meetings. Did I understand you well? Because it was part of my question, where would be present Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Koljevic, frequent presence of others during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Sometimes there were others too. Sometimes Krajisnik was there. Sometimes Mico Stanisic. Sometimes Prime Minister Djeric. Well, perhaps in some situations even some other ministers. I don't know. Well, depended on the issues that were being discussed. Sometimes this man, the foreign minister, would be there, Buha. If it had to do with talks with some foreign delegations or, say, Cutileiro or whoever else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Subotic, we'll stop for the day as far as your testimony is concerned. We are not sitting tomorrow because there is a Plenary meeting of the Judges so we have one day of not sitting. We would like to see you back, although in a different courtroom, Courtroom III, at 11.00 this Friday. Mr. Subotic, I have to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give next Friday. Then we would like to see you back on Friday. Would you please be so kind to follow Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, Mr. Registrar, I received a signed B/C/S copy of the statement of Mr. Subotic which was provided, number C3. I've now given it to you. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour there is one point, Your Honour. Your Honours, understandably Your Honours gave instructions that Mr. Krajisnik's privilege line was to be removed during the course of his evidence. It hasn't been restored but we would understand that the Trial Chamber would take whatever steps were necessary to give whatever directions were necessary for its restoration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give the necessary information, as far as the Chamber is concerned, of course, we are not competent to further deal with the matter apart from what we would oppose against or what we are not responsible for any other -- any other circumstances that might perhaps not but might --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood. It's -- in effect, it's -- it's if you like a revocation or an indication that the Trial Chamber's direction in relation to that has now expired or is revoked or whatever the appropriate course. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will pay proper attention to that. We will then adjourn until next Friday, 11.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of June, 2006, at 11.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
